title: Promises
summary: Create promises, chain results with then and handle failures with catch.

quiz.q: A promise can be in one of three states. Which list is correct?
quiz.explain: A promise starts as pending. Later it becomes fulfilled (it has a value) or rejected (it has an error). After that it never changes.

quiz.q: What does this program print? Write the two words separated by a space.
quiz.explain: `then` callbacks always run later, after the current code is finished. So `first` prints, then the chain produces 10.

quiz.q: Complete the chain so errors are handled.
quiz.explain: `.catch` runs when any earlier step in the chain rejects, so one `catch` at the end covers the whole chain.

quiz.q: Put the lines in order to build a promise that resolves after 100 ms.
quiz.explain: The executor function receives `resolve`. Calling it, here from inside the timer, fulfills the promise with a value.

quiz.q: Inside `new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...)`, how do you signal failure?
quiz.explain: `reject(error)` marks the promise as rejected. Use an `Error` object so the message and stack are available to `catch`.

exercise.task:
In `promises.js`, write three functions:

- `wait(ms, value)` returns a promise that fulfills with `value` after `ms` milliseconds.
- `checkAge(age)` returns a promise. It fulfills with `'allowed'` when `age >= 18`, otherwise it rejects with `new Error('too young')`.
- `describeAge(age)` uses `checkAge(age)` with `.then` and `.catch` and returns a promise that always fulfills: with `'Welcome'` when allowed, or with the error's message when not.
hints: Wrap the code in `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })`. Call `resolve(...)` or `reject(...)` exactly once.
